coverage: 12 public learning projects, curated from their upstream READMEs and verified source paths. Start small, follow one slice, then move to a capstone. Links need internet; repository code, assets and dependencies are not bundled.

projects.title: micrograd
projects.summary: A compact automatic-differentiation engine lets you inspect how a value keeps track of the operations that produced it.
projects.why: Its small scalar engine makes the path from arithmetic to gradients unusually easy to follow.
projects.requirements: Python and the foundations gradient lesson. Reading the engine needs no GPU; upstream tests use PyTorch.
steps: Open Value.__mul__ in engine.py. For a=2 and b=3, write the forward value and both local derivatives before reading the backward callback.
Trace backward through one multiplication and one addition. Draw the dependency graph and explain why contributions to the same input must add.
Compare your pencil-and-paper gradients with one case in test/test_engine.py. Change one input in your own small fixture and predict the result.
projects.deliverable: An annotated three-operation graph with predicted gradients and one reproducible comparison.
projects.evidence: Public README reviewed and starting-file path verified on 2026-10-05. The first task is a source walkthrough; upstream installation and execution were not tested here.

projects.title: TodoMVC · React
projects.summary: One familiar to-do application exposes state updates, filtering and persistence without a large product domain.
projects.why: The shared application specification gives you observable behavior to compare against each implementation.
projects.requirements: JavaScript objects and the web-state lesson. Read the reducer first; running the React example needs its documented Node setup.
steps: Open the reducer and choose one action. Write a before/after state containing two to-dos, without opening the rest of the application yet.
Follow that action from its UI control into the reducer. Identify what changes and which object or array must remain unchanged.
Use app-spec.md to choose one edge case, such as editing to an empty title. Draft an interaction test and compare it with the implementation.
projects.deliverable: A single action trace and an observable UI test for one edge case.
projects.evidence: Public README reviewed and starting-file path verified on 2026-10-05. The first task is a source walkthrough; upstream installation and execution were not tested here.

projects.title: Gymnasium · CartPole
projects.summary: A standard environment API gives you a smaller first RL project before moving to emulator training.
projects.why: CartPole makes observation, action, reward and episode endings concrete in a single environment module.
projects.requirements: The RL environment lesson. Source reading is CPU-only; local rendering needs the classic-control extra described upstream.
steps: Find reset and step. List the observation components and legal actions; separate the agent’s choice from the environment’s state update.
Follow one step to its reward and termination condition. Then locate where an external time limit is applied outside the base environment.
Write a seeded random-policy evaluation plan: episode length, total reward and both ending flags. Keep training out of this first experiment.
projects.deliverable: A one-page environment contract and a baseline evaluation record you can reproduce.
projects.evidence: Public README reviewed and starting-file path verified on 2026-10-05. The first task is a source walkthrough; upstream installation and execution were not tested here.

projects.title: PyTorch · regression example
projects.summary: An official regression example connects model parameters, a loss and optimizer updates in a real training script.
projects.why: It is a focused bridge from the workshop’s small regression exercise to a complete source file.
projects.requirements: PyTorch tensor and optimizer lessons. Inspect the synthetic regression example before trying examples that download datasets.
steps: Locate model creation, generated examples and the loss in regression/main.py. Write the shape and role of each input.
Find zero_grad, backward and step. Explain why that order matters and what would change if gradients accumulated accidentally.
Plan a small repeatable experiment changing only the learning rate. Record seed, step count and held-out error before comparing outcomes.
projects.deliverable: An annotated training loop and a controlled one-variable experiment.
projects.evidence: Public README reviewed and starting-file path verified on 2026-10-05. The first task is a source walkthrough; upstream installation and execution were not tested here.

projects.title: Keras · engineering introduction
projects.summary: A narrated Keras guide connects model construction, training and evaluation with a readable Python source.
projects.why: The explanations and code live together, so you can study one section without rebuilding the documentation site.
projects.requirements: TensorFlow tensors and the Keras model lesson. Choose the TensorFlow backend; upstream sections may download datasets.
steps: Open the guide’s first model-building section. Identify inputs, layers and output shape; stop before running a full training example.
Trace compile, fit and evaluate in the relevant section. Explain the optimizer, loss and metric roles in your own words.
Adapt only the model-shape idea to a tiny synthetic fixture. Compare one prediction before and after a controlled training step.
projects.deliverable: A model shape diagram and a small TensorFlow-backed training comparison.
projects.evidence: Public README reviewed and starting-file path verified on 2026-10-05. The first task is a source walkthrough; upstream installation and execution were not tested here.

projects.title: smolagents
projects.summary: An agent library makes the orchestration loop, tool calls and recorded steps available to inspect.
projects.why: You can trace the harness separately from model quality and begin with a fake model response.
projects.requirements: Harness state and tool-contract lessons. Read source or use mocked tools first; live agents need a model and may invoke external tools.
steps: Find the main agent run loop and its step limit. Sketch the states for continuing, finishing and failing before reading every helper.
Trace one proposed tool call into validation and execution. Identify which errors become recorded observations and which stop the run.
Design a fake-model test with an invalid tool name and another with too many steps. State the expected trace and stopping behavior.
projects.deliverable: A run-loop state chart and two deterministic harness test cases.
projects.evidence: Public README reviewed and starting-file path verified on 2026-10-05. The first task is a source walkthrough; upstream installation and execution were not tested here.

projects.title: Full Stack FastAPI Template
projects.summary: A concrete API route connects validation, identity, storage and a React client in a larger application.
projects.why: The item route is a manageable slice of a complete service; start there instead of booting the entire stack.
projects.requirements: Backend validation and web-state lessons. The full app needs the documented database and service setup; the first walkthrough is read-only.
steps: Read one item route and its request/response model. Write the contract and identify where the current user affects access.
Locate the matching frontend call and trace loading, success and failure states. Keep an API error distinct from an empty list.
Choose a route test and describe an additional invalid-input or ownership case using synthetic users and items.
projects.deliverable: One end-to-end request diagram and a concrete API regression-test case.
projects.evidence: Public README reviewed and starting-file path verified on 2026-10-05. The first task is a source walkthrough; upstream installation and execution were not tested here.

projects.title: LlamaIndex · document schema
projects.summary: Document and node types provide a useful entry into source identity, metadata and retrieval evidence.
projects.why: Starting with data structures avoids requiring a hosted model to understand a retrieval pipeline.
projects.requirements: Document and chunking lessons. Use synthetic text; live embedding or cloud parsing examples have separate setup requirements.
steps: Locate Document and TextNode in the core schema. Identify text, identity, metadata and relationships, and explain why those fields differ.
Sketch how a document becomes two overlapping chunks while retaining a link to its source. Use five invented sentences.
Create three queries with known relevant chunk IDs and calculate recall at k. Explain why retrieval success does not itself verify a generated answer.
projects.deliverable: A document-to-chunk diagram and a tiny retrieval evaluation table.
projects.evidence: Public README and schema path reviewed on 2026-10-05. The README describes a shift in company focus toward parsing; this walkthrough targets the available OSS core schema, not a cloud product.

projects.title: Temporal · retry example
projects.summary: A small workflow example demonstrates retries as an explicit execution policy.
projects.why: One activity failure is enough to study attempts, retry policy and durable workflow behavior.
projects.requirements: Python async basics and bounded retries. Reading needs no server; execution requires the upstream Temporal CLI/dev-server setup.
steps: Open hello_activity_retry.py and identify the workflow, activity and retry policy. Describe what intentionally fails and when it succeeds.
Write the sequence of attempts on paper. Explain why a retried activity that writes externally must account for repeated execution.
Design a test for an exhausted retry policy and another for an idempotent repeated request. Record final status separately from attempt count.
projects.deliverable: An attempt timeline and two failure-focused test specifications.
projects.evidence: Public README reviewed and starting-file path verified on 2026-10-05. The first task is a source walkthrough; upstream installation and execution were not tested here.

projects.title: PokeRL · Pokémon Red
projects.summary: An emulator-based RL project extends the environment contract to richer observations, reward shaping and long episodes.
projects.why: Keep PokeRL as the learning journey and use the credited PokémonRedExperiments source for the implementation walkthrough.
projects.requirements: Complete the RL path and start with Gymnasium first. Actual emulator runs need user-supplied game assets and upstream dependencies; source study does not.
steps: Open the upstream v2 environment. Trace reset and one step, listing action, observation, reward components and stopping signals.
Choose one reward component and explain the behavior it encourages. Invent a failure case where improving that reward would not imply useful game progress.
Plan evaluation with fixed seeds, a random-policy baseline, checkpoint identity and separate metrics for rewards and task progress.
projects.deliverable: An environment/reward diagram and a reproducible evaluation plan before attempting training.
projects.evidence: PokeRL’s public README is a brief project link and credits the original work. The starting file is in PWhiddy/PokemonRedExperiments (MIT), verified on 2026-10-05. No game assets or upstream code are bundled.

projects.title: Vigil at Home
projects.summary: A desktop security application offers an advanced study of local events, deterministic rules, AI explanations and human decisions.
projects.why: Trace a single alert to separate detection logic from agent recommendations and user-controlled actions.
projects.requirements: Harness, backend and UI-state paths. Begin with source and tests; installing privileged helpers is outside this learning walkthrough.
steps: Read the desktop architecture and choose one alert flow. Draw event → rule decision → stored result → UI, marking process boundaries.
Find where an AI recommendation reaches the interface. Compare its authority with the user’s action and the deterministic rule engine.
Design a synthetic UI test for unavailable explanation service, duplicate alert and app restart. Define expected state without operating on real security events.
projects.deliverable: A process/authority diagram and three synthetic acceptance cases.
projects.evidence: Public README and desktop entry point checked on 2026-10-05. Upstream describes an early-alpha macOS app; no release, helper installation or live detection was verified here.

projects.title: NVIDIA · vector addition
projects.summary: A native CUDA sample connects allocation, transfer, kernel launch and result verification in C++.
projects.why: Vector addition is a small enough kernel to compare directly with the workshop’s simulated indexing exercises.
projects.requirements: The CUDA path and basic C++ reading. Native execution requires supported NVIDIA hardware and toolkit; a Mac can still be used for the source walkthrough.
steps: Trace the host-side allocation, copy, kernel launch and cleanup. Label which pointer belongs to which memory location.
Calculate thread indices for a five-element vector using four threads per block. Find the kernel’s guard for the extra threads.
Read the result verification and error handling. Write a later hardware experiment that separates correctness checks from timing measurements.
projects.deliverable: A host/device memory diagram and an indexing trace; hardware timing is a separate optional follow-up.
projects.evidence: Public README reviewed and starting-file path verified on 2026-10-05. The first task is a source walkthrough; upstream installation and execution were not tested here.
